title: Floating-point precision (0.1 + 0.2)
description: JS numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 and most decimal fractions can't be represented exactly in binary — compare with an epsilon, round with toFixed, or scale to integers for money math.

notes: Why it happens: 0.1 and 0.2 are infinite repeating fractions in binary, so the stored IEEE 754 double is the nearest representable value — the rounding error surfaces on add.
`Number.EPSILON` (~2.22e-16) is the gap between 1 and the next representable double; for values away from 1 you usually want a friendlier tolerance like 1e-9.
`===` between two floats is almost always wrong unless one side is an integer literal you control end-to-end.
`toFixed(n)` returns a STRING, not a number. Useful for display or string-compare, never for further arithmetic without re-parsing.
For money, store integer cents (or use a library like decimal.js / big.js). Round each scaled term — `0.1 * 100` can already be 10.000000000000002.
The trap appears in many languages — it's not a JS bug, it's IEEE 754. Python's `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004` too.

questions.explain: IEEE 754 can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly in binary — the sum lands at the nearest representable double, which prints with the trailing `...004`.
The left side is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3 — strict equality on floats almost always loses to rounding error.

questions.q: Which is the safest way to check that two floats are 'equal' within tolerance?
questions.explain: Compare the absolute difference against an epsilon. `Object.is` is even stricter than `===` for numbers and doesn't help with rounding error.
`toFixed` returns a string. Useful for display or string-compare, but you'll need `Number(...)` or `+...` to do further math.

questions.q: Why store money as integer cents instead of dollar floats?
options: Integers are faster on modern CPUs
Floats can lose pennies because 0.1, 0.2, etc. aren't exactly representable
questions.explain: Summing 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 as floats can drift away from 0.6. Scaling to integer cents (and rounding each scaled term) sidesteps the rounding error entirely.

exercises.prompt: Show the rounding error directly: print the sum, then the strict-equality check against 0.3.

exercises.prompt: Fix the comparison with an epsilon tolerance. Use the absolute difference and a friendly 1e-9 threshold.
Money math: sum two prices via scale-and-integer to avoid pennies drift. Round each scaled term before adding.

L3.prompt: Write `nearlyEqual(a, b, eps)` that returns true when |a - b| <= eps. Then log: the raw value of `0.1 + 0.2`, whether `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3`, whether `nearlyEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, 1e-9)`, and whether `nearlyEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.4, 1e-9)` — one result per line.
hints: `Math.abs(a - b)` collapses both signs of the gap into one nonnegative number.
`<=` (not `<`) is the conventional comparison so exact-equal values also pass.
1e-9 is a friendlier tolerance than `Number.EPSILON` (~2.22e-16) when the values aren't right at 1.0.
